title: The Best Policy When the Model Is Known: Value Iteration, the Greedy Move, and the Route the Discount Chooses

questions.question: When the chances and rewards of a task are known, how is the best policy found?
options: By trying every policy and keeping the best
By sweeping the equation for the best value until it settles, then taking the greedy move in each cell
By training a network on demonstrations
By choosing the shortest path
questions.explanation: Value iteration finds the best value for every cell at once; the best policy is a lookup on it.

questions.question: With gamma 0.95, what was the optimal value at the start, and how did it compare?
options: -13.357, the same as the random policy
-5.245, worse than going round
-5.745, the same as going round
-5.245, at least as good as going round (-5.745) and the random policy (-13.357)
questions.explanation: No policy beats the optimum, at the start or anywhere.

questions.question: With gamma 0.80, what did the greedy policy do from the start, and how did it fare?
options: It went the long way round; 95 percent of runs reached the goal
It took the corridor; 54 percent reached the goal
It stayed put
It fell in a pit every time
questions.explanation: A low discount makes a pit on the next step count far more than the length of the way.

questions.question: With gamma 0.95, what changed?
options: Nothing
It took the corridor beside the pits: 54 percent reached the goal, with a mean return of -5.16
It refused to move
It reached the goal on every run
questions.explanation: It weighs the whole path, and the short corridor is worth the risk of a pit to it.

questions.question: Why is the discount an engineering decision and not a constant?
options: Because it must always be 0.99
Because it only changes how fast value iteration runs
Because it changes which policy is best, here how much risk is taken
Because it sets the step cost
questions.explanation: Leaving it at a usual value is choosing a route without looking.

questions.question: The optimal policy reaches the goal on only half its runs, and the robot must almost never fall. What is the right fix?
options: Make the falls a constraint the policy must meet, not just part of the average
Run more sweeps
Lower the reward of the goal
Use the random policy
questions.explanation: The expected return can trade a fall for a shorter path. A limit on falls is a separate requirement (39-09).
